1 · Start here

Use one chain for almost every question

Lung position / lesion→alveolar expansion + pressure→capillary patency→V vs Q→V/Q→PAO₂ / PACO₂→arterial effect

Professor emphasis: do not memorize “apex high, base low” without the why. Dr. C repeatedly ties the gradient back to the “slinky lung,” gravitational blood hydrostatic pressure, and the fact that perfusion changes by a greater magnitude than ventilation.

Fast topic map

Normal: zones 1→3, pressure relationships, V/Q gradient.

Mismatch: dead space ↔ high V/Q ↔ match ↔ low V/Q ↔ shunt.

Bridge to next lecture: A–a gradient = PAO₂ − PaO₂.

2 · Mechanisms

Normal physiology → predictable V/Q

Selectable lung-zone explorer

Relative trends in an upright lung

Apex
Middle
Base

Ventilation: ↑ from apex → base

Perfusion: ↑↑ from apex → base

V/Q: ↓ from apex → base

Key causal point: Q increases to a greater magnitude than V.

Pressure rules before you calculate anything

Zone 1: PA > Pa > Pv
Alveolus can compress capillary → low flow.
Zone 2: Pa > PA > Pv
Arterial pressure opens upstream vessel; alveolar pressure still limits downstream flow.
Zone 3: Pa > Pv > PA
Vascular pressures dominate → most patent capillary → high flow.

Gas-direction rules

Alveolus

Move toward dead space: less perfusion → less CO₂ delivery and less O₂ removal → PAO₂ ↑, PACO₂ ↓.

Move toward shunt: less ventilation → alveolar gas equilibrates toward mixed venous blood → PAO₂ ↓, PACO₂ ↑.

A–a bridge

Lecture rule: pure hypoventilation can lower both PAO₂ and PaO₂ together, leaving the A–a difference relatively normal. V/Q mismatch separates them and widens the gradient.

Clarification Slide 25 uses an idealized A–a = 0 model. In real healthy adults, a small physiologic A–a gradient exists and rises with age; see Sources.

6 · Lecture figures

Blind first, source after reveal

Figure challenge A

Question: What pressure relationship and perfusion state should you predict in the lowest region?

Reveal explanation + source

Lowest region = zone 3. Pa > Pv > PA; vessels are most patent and perfusion is greatest.

Source: Respiratory_lecture_4_VQ_POST.pptx, slide 11. Cropped to remove answer-revealing text.

Figure challenge B

Question: Which end has smaller resting alveoli, greater compliance, and greater ventilation?

Reveal explanation + source

The base. Basal alveoli are less expanded at rest, sit on a more compliant part of the curve, and expand more during inspiration.

Source: Respiratory_lecture_4_VQ_POST.pptx, slide 17. Text labels removed for blind retrieval.

Figure challenge C

Question: Use the displayed values to calculate the A–a difference.

Reveal explanation + source

PAO₂ 100 − PaO₂ 80 = 20 mm Hg. The poorly ventilated compartment lowers mixed arterial oxygen after blood mixes.

Source: Respiratory_lecture_4_VQ_POST.pptx, slide 26. Top answer line intentionally cropped.

8 · Exam sheet

Printable final-review sheet

Zones

  • Zone 1: PA > Pa > Pv; large alveoli; lowest compliance; low Q; V/Q high (~3.3 in lecture).
  • Zone 2: Pa > PA > Pv; V/Q ~1.
  • Zone 3: Pa > Pv > PA; smaller/more compliant alveoli; highest V and Q; V/Q low (~0.63).

Mismatch endpoints

  • Dead space: V present, Q absent → V/Q ∞ → PAO₂ ~150, PACO₂ ~0.
  • Shunt: V absent, Q present → V/Q 0 → gas approaches mixed venous (~40 O₂ / ~45 CO₂).
  • High V/Q: O₂ ↑, CO₂ ↓.
  • Low V/Q: O₂ ↓, CO₂ ↑.

Mechanism rules

  • Base ventilates more because alveoli are less expanded at rest and more compliant.
  • Base perfuses more because gravity increases vascular hydrostatic pressure and recruitment.
  • Q increases more than V from apex → base, so V/Q falls.
  • Expanded alveoli can physically compress adjacent capillaries.

A–a

  • A–a = PAO₂ − PaO₂.
  • Hypoventilation alone: both fall together → gradient relatively normal.
  • V/Q mismatch / shunt: separation grows → widened gradient.
  • Lecture slide 26 example: 100 − 80 = 20 mm Hg.

Common traps

  • Do not confuse pressure symbols: on the lung-zone slide, PA, Pa, Pv are hydrostatic pressures—not oxygen partial pressures.
  • PAO₂ is alveolar oxygen partial pressure; PaO₂ is systemic arterial oxygen partial pressure.
  • Ideal local V/Q = 1; lecture whole-lung average ≈ 0.8.
  • Zone 3 has greater absolute V and Q, yet a lower ratio because Q rises more.
9 · Sources + clarifications

What was used, and what needed clarification

Lecture materials used

  • Respiratory_lecture_4_VQ_POST.pptx — primary figures, pressure relationships, V/Q values, A–a examples.
  • Ventilation Perfusio-transcript.txt — professor emphasis, causal explanations, examples, “teach it/draw it” priorities.
  • Respiratory_Physiology_Lecture_4_-_Ventilation_Perfusion_Mismatch_Objectives.docx — scope and required comparisons.
  • Ventilation_Perfusion_Mismatch_-_Practice_Questions.V2.docx — 3 professor questions and answer key.

Meaningful clarifications

1 · V/Q average The transcript contains a spoken line suggesting “1.6” across two lungs, then “0.8 in each lung.” The slide itself states average V/Q across the entire lung = 0.8, and NCBI likewise describes net V/Q ≈ 0.8 from ~4 L/min alveolar ventilation / ~5 L/min pulmonary blood flow. This guide uses 0.8 whole-lung average.

2 · A–a = 0 on slide 25 The professor’s slide is an idealized teaching model. Clinically, healthy people generally have a small physiologic A–a gradient that increases with age (roughly 10–15 mm Hg in a common reference).

3 · “hypokalemic shock” The transcript says “hypokalemic shock” while discussing hemorrhage, severe blood-volume loss, and falling pressure. That context is consistent with hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock, which is the term used in this guide.

External verification: NCBI Bookshelf: Partial Pressure of Oxygen; NCBI Bookshelf: Alveolar–Arterial Oxygen Gradient; and NCBI Bookshelf: Shock. These clarifications are supplemental and do not replace the professor’s tested lecture framing.
